result: The authors developed an all-optical electrophysiology platform (Optopatch) by engineering HEK293 cells to stably express NaV1.7, CheRiff (blue-light activated channelrhodopsin), QuasAr2 (voltage indicator), and transiently express Kir2.1 (inward rectifier K+ channel). The system was characterized by patch clamp, showing CheRiff activation at 488 nm with EPD50 of 20 mW/cm², NaV1.7 peak current density of -61.4 ± 13.6 pA/pF at -20 mV, and resting potential of -97.2 ± 2.2 mV in 2 mM K+.
evaluation: Claims C7, C34, C63, C65-C78 collectively describe the construction and characterization of the NaV1.7-OS HEK cell line. The experimental data in Figures 1 and 2, along with patch clamp measurements, provide strong support for the successful engineering and functional characterization of all four components. The measurements are quantitative with appropriate sample sizes (n=5-11 cells) and error reporting.

result: Brief blue light pulses (20 ms, 50 mW/cm²) reliably triggered single action potentials with firing threshold of -48.0 ± 1.2 mV, peak depolarization of +30.1 ± 3.7 mV, and APD50 of 33.5 ± 3.3 ms. Steady-state blue illumination induced graded depolarizations up to -25.8 ± 6.2 mV. QuasAr2 fluorescence faithfully reproduced both action potential waveforms and subthreshold depolarizations.
evaluation: Claims C38-C44 and C79-C86 describe the optical stimulation and recording capabilities. Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 provide direct experimental evidence with simultaneous patch clamp validation. The quantitative parameters are well-defined with appropriate statistical reporting (mean ± s.e.m., n=5 cells), supporting the claim that optical measurements faithfully reproduce electrical signals.

result: Voltage spike amplitude measured optically was smoothly and monotonically related to NaV1.7 current density measured by patch clamp. Individual cells showed graded spike amplitude as a function of NaV1.7 capacity with 8% standard deviation in spike height at 50% channel block.
evaluation: Claims C87-C90 establish the quantitative relationship between optical and electrical measurements. Figure 2—figure supplement 2C demonstrates the monotonic relationship, and Figure 2—figure supplement 3 shows single-cell measurements. The experimental design using amitriptyline to induce varying degrees of channel block is appropriate, and the 8% variability at 50% block (n=5 cells) demonstrates good precision.

result: Phototoxicity testing showed minimal temperature rise (<0.3°C) in 35 mm dishes and 2.5 ± 0.4°C in 35 s in 384-well plates under 400 W/cm² red illumination. Cells maintained spiking capability for 10 min with SNR dropping from 107 ± 2 to 73 ± 2.6. High SNR (99.8 ± 3.3) was achieved at 400 W/cm² at 100 Hz frame rate.
evaluation: Claims C91-C101 address phototoxicity concerns. Figure 2—figure supplement 4 provides comprehensive data on temperature rise, photobleaching, and SNR across different conditions. The measurements include appropriate controls and replicates (n=4-8). The authors appropriately limited protocols to <35 s to avoid thermal artifacts, demonstrating careful experimental design.

result: Optical electrophysiology recapitulated voltage-clamp protocols for studying use-dependent sodium channel block. Lidocaine (200 μM) showed activity-dependent block at 4 Hz and 8 Hz but not 2 Hz. Simultaneous patch clamp and fluorescence recordings showed close correspondence with residual variations equivalent to 2.8 mV in 200 Hz bandwidth.
evaluation: Claims C8, C103-C108 demonstrate the ability to replicate standard electrophysiology protocols. Figure 3A shows clear use-dependent block patterns, and Figure 3B validates optical measurements against patch clamp. The 2.8 mV residual variation is acceptably small for detecting action potentials. The use of lidocaine as a well-characterized use-dependent blocker provides strong validation.

result: Amitriptyline showed strong state-dependent binding with IC50 varying from 11.7 ± 1.6 μM (20 ms prepulse) to 1.6 ± 0.1 μM (500 ms prepulse). TTX showed modest state dependence with IC50 of 126 ± 13 nM (20 ms) to 62 ± 5.8 nM (500 ms), consistent with prior patch clamp findings.
evaluation: Claims C109-C114 demonstrate state-dependent pharmacology measurements. Figure 3C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 show dose-response curves with varying prepulse durations. The IC50 values are reported with appropriate error estimates from Hill equation fits (n=3-6 wells per point). Consistency with prior patch clamp literature (C111, C114) provides external validation.

result: Recovery from inactivation assays showed DMSO-treated cells recovered within 40 ms, carbamazepine blocked recovery at 40 ms but not 80 ms, and amitriptyline dramatically slowed half-recovery time to 280 ± 36 ms at 3 μM, indicating slow dissociation at -97 mV resting potential.
evaluation: Claims C115-C119 describe recovery kinetics measurements. Figure 3E,F provides clear experimental data with appropriate sample sizes (n=9 wells per point). The interpretation that slow recovery reflects slow drug dissociation (C119) is a reasonable inference from the data, though it assumes no other rate-limiting steps in channel repriming.

result: Carbamazepine reduced the overlap between activation and inactivation (window current) by left-shifting the fast inactivation curve without altering activation. While optical electrophysiology cannot quantify the window current, it can identify the qualitative mechanistic feature, sign, and approximate magnitude of the effect.
evaluation: Claims C125-C127 describe window current measurements. Figure 3G,H shows the effect of carbamazepine on activation/inactivation curves, consistent with prior electrophysiology literature. The authors appropriately acknowledge the limitation that optical methods cannot quantify window current (C126) while demonstrating they can detect qualitative changes (C127). This honest assessment of method limitations strengthens credibility.

result: PF-04856264 binding to NaV1.7 is strongly voltage-dependent. At -97 mV resting potential (2 mM K+), even 2 s prepulses failed to induce block at 100 nM. Elevating bath K+ to 8 mM (depolarizing to ~-70 mV) enabled IC50 of 43 nM with 2 s prepulse. Sustained baseline depolarization was more effective than brief strong depolarization due to slow binding kinetics.
evaluation: Claims C10, C133-C140 characterize PF-04856264 mechanism. Figure 4A,B,C provides comprehensive dose-response data under different conditions. The hypothesis that resting potential differences explain discrepancies with literature (C134) is tested experimentally by varying extracellular K+, showing Nernstian behavior (C135). The IC50 of 43 nM at -70 mV is close to the literature value of 28 nM, validating the approach. The conclusion about slow binding kinetics (C140) is well-supported by the prepulse duration experiments.

result: A pilot screen of 320 FDA-approved compounds at 10 μM stratified drugs by binding mechanism and kinetics using two parameters (σ, Γ). The screen achieved Z' factor of 0.57 and 12.2% hit rate. Doxepin clustered with amitriptyline controls, consistent with their structural similarity. Compounds showed diverse patterns including monotonic decay and alternans.
evaluation: Claims C11-C12, C142-C161 describe the high-throughput screen. Figure 5A,B,C shows clear separation of controls and diverse hit patterns. The Z' factor of 0.57 (C155) is within acceptable range for HTS (C156). The blinded identification of doxepin near amitriptyline (C153-C154) provides strong validation of the method's ability to classify compounds by mechanism. The 12.2% hit rate (C157) is consistent with NaV channels being promiscuous binders (C158).

result: Alternans compounds (isradipine, iloperidone) showed half-maximal recovery in 20 ms, while strong blockers (amitriptyline, trifluoperazine) showed <50% recovery in 256 ms, compared to 4.5 ms for controls. Compounds clustering nearby in optical (σ, Γ) space showed similar effects by patch clamp.
evaluation: Claims C162-C166 validate the optical screen against patch clamp. Figure 5D,E shows recovery kinetics measured by voltage clamp for selected hits. The hypothesis about alternans compounds (C162) is tested and confirmed. The concordance between optical clustering and patch clamp measurements (C166) provides strong validation of the screening approach.

result: Testing hits on NaV1.5-OS cells showed all non-selective hits arranged similarly for both NaV1.5 and NaV1.7, while PF-04856264 and TTX (1 μM each) clustered with negative controls for NaV1.5, demonstrating subtype selectivity.
evaluation: Claims C167-C171 demonstrate subtype selectivity testing. Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 show the NaV1.5 results. The observation that most hits lack selectivity (C168) while known selective compounds (PF-04856264, TTX) cluster with controls (C170-C171) validates the platform's ability to detect selectivity. This is consistent with established knowledge that NaV1.7-selective compounds are rare (C169).

result: Off-target testing showed 6 of 7 compounds had minimal effect (<7% of TTX) on Kir2.1, CheRiff, or QuasAr2. Carbamazepine reduced QuasAr2 voltage sensitivity by 17%, but this had no effect on activity-dependent block assays due to spike height normalization.
evaluation: Claims C175-C182 address potential confounds from off-target effects. Figure 5—figure supplement 2 provides comprehensive testing with both optical and patch clamp validation. The finding that carbamazepine affects QuasAr2 (C180) but not the normalized assay results (C181) demonstrates the robustness of the analysis approach. Sample sizes are adequate (n=9-10 wells, n=3-4 cells for patch clamp).

result: KV4.3 was successfully expressed in NaV1.5-OS cells, showing maximum current density of 218 pA/pF, fast activation (τact = 0.69 ms), and double exponential inactivation (τfast = 51 ms, τslow = 352 ms). HpTx2 blocked KV4.3 with IC50 of 252 nM, consistent with literature, and altered action potential waveform as expected.
evaluation: Claims C183-C194 demonstrate extension to KV4.3. Figure 6A-D provides comprehensive characterization including voltage clamp, optical recordings, and dose-response for HpTx2. The kinetic parameters match literature values (C188), and the IC50 of 252 nM is consistent with prior work (C194). The dramatic change in action potential waveform (C190) and effects of HpTx2 (C192-C193) are clearly demonstrated.

result: Optopatch assays provide a favorable tradeoff between throughput and information content for NaV channel studies. Despite variable expression levels, the assays accurately probe state-dependent pharmacology and report binding affinities and kinetics by averaging over large cell numbers and using protocols insensitive to expression variations.
evaluation: Claims C13, C197-C200 represent the main conclusions. The experimental data throughout the manuscript (Figures 2-5) demonstrate accurate measurements of IC50 values, state-dependent binding, recovery kinetics, and mechanism classification. The validation against patch clamp (Figures 3B, 5D,E) and concordance with literature values support accuracy claims. The methodological insights about averaging and normalization (C199-C200) are well-supported by the experimental design.

result: Stimulus and data analysis protocols were developed that are robust to cellular variation. While whole-cell voltage clamp remains the gold standard for absolute accuracy, optical electrophysiology provides a favorable tradeoff between accuracy and throughput.
evaluation: Claims C47-C48 summarize the methodological contribution and positioning relative to patch clamp. The robustness is demonstrated throughout by consistent results across wells and validation experiments. The acknowledgment that patch clamp remains the gold standard (C48) while claiming a favorable tradeoff is appropriately balanced and supported by the comparative data.

result: The authors speculate that optical electrophysiology may be applicable to other voltage-gated channels including other NaV subtypes (NaV1.1-1.9), CaV channels, and delayed rectifier K+ channels (hERG, KV7), based on demonstrated success with NaV1.7, NaV1.5, and KV4.3, and citing prior work on CaV channels.
evaluation: Claims C14, C196, C230-C239 are largely speculative about future applications. While the success with three channel types (NaV1.7, NaV1.5, KV4.3) provides some support, most claims about other channels are based on citations to prior work or logical extrapolation rather than direct experimental evidence in this manuscript. The limitation noted for KV4.3 screening (C196) highlights that extension to other channels may require additional optimization.

result: The authors position Optopatch relative to existing methods: flux-based assays offer high throughput but only probe steady-state behavior; automated patch clamp offers voltage control but has lower throughput, higher cost, and membrane perturbation issues. Optopatch provides detailed mechanistic information, HTS compatibility, and is non-invasive. Current throughput is ~3 s/well (384-well plate in ~20 min) with potential for improvement.
evaluation: Claims C201-C218 provide context and comparison to other methods. The characterization of flux-based assays (C201-C203) and automated patch clamp (C204-C210) represents established knowledge supported by citations. The claims about Optopatch advantages (C211-C213) are supported by the experimental data. The throughput measurements (C214) are directly demonstrated. Speculations about future improvements (C215, C218) are appropriately qualified.

result: Illumination intensities for Arch-based GEVIs are 10-100-fold higher than GFP-based indicators. A cited study showed 200 W/cm² at 488 nm caused 100% cell death/freezing while 5900 W/cm² at 640 nm caused undetectable death in U2OS cells. The observed viability at 400 W/cm², 640 nm is consistent with these results.
evaluation: Claims C219-C223 address phototoxicity concerns by comparison to literature. The characterization of illumination requirements (C219) is established knowledge. The cited phototoxicity study (C220-C222) provides context for the safety of red illumination. The inference that the authors' observations are consistent with literature (C223) is reasonable given their measurements of cell viability and the cited wavelength-dependent toxicity data.

result: The authors speculate that screening approaches could be adapted to work with red-shifted voltage-sensitive dyes, which would offer more homogeneous signals, easier cell line switching, and potentially lower illumination intensity. However, existing dyes (PGH1, Di-2-ANBDQPQ) have crosstalk with channelrhodopsin activation and are not commercially available.
evaluation: Claims C224-C229 are speculative about using voltage-sensitive dyes instead of genetically encoded indicators. The potential advantages (C225-C227) are logical but untested. The limitations of existing dyes (C228-C229) are supported by citations. Without experimental demonstration, these remain speculations about alternative approaches rather than established results.
